utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, everybody. Since we are going to hear some objection from Mr. Robinson, we found it to be better to start without the witness. So, Mr. Robinson. Just a second. Before we hear from you, Mr. Robinson, I have to note that since Judge Robinson -- I'm sorry, Judge Morrison cannot be us to perform his official function, so we'll be sitting here today pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It may well be that it's better we deal with this issue on Monday, when Judge Morrison is back, but I'll leave that up to you. The nature of the objection is, in a sense, a request that we somehow revisit what we did yesterday and go back to where we were the day before yesterday with respect to the ruling on admissibility of documents. I believe that under Rule 89(C), three criteria for admitting documents is reliability, relevance, and probative value. And things that are not criteria necessarily are that the witness have personal knowledge of the document or that the document itself be true. In fact, in some cases the parties may wish to introduce a document to show that it wasn't true. So, now, the question of whether a document has probative value, it seems that the Chamber's -- the parties, at least, believed that a document would have probative value if it was otherwise reliable and relevant and had something to do with the witness's testimony, whether or not the witness could speak to that document directly or not. The Chamber seems to have adopted a position that only those things that are consistent with the witness's testimony can be probative, and we think that that creates an unfairness that will allow only documents that bolster the credibility of a witness to be admitted, and those that impeach the credibility of a witness will not be admitted. And if we look at some examples from this witness and the previous witness, Ms. Zaimovic, I think we can see how the same type of document can be applied in those two ways. For example, an order of the Army of the Republika Srpska, which you admitted for this witness, David Harland, because it was consistent with his testimony, yet we had orders from the army that were inconsistent with the testimony of Ms. Zaimovic. She seemed to want to deny that there were any Muslim Army operations around the hospital, yet we had orders showing that it was crawling with army people and that they were using it as a base to shell Serb positions and conduct military operations. So the same kind of document, an order from an army, is admissible when it's consistent with the witness's testimony, and not admissible when it impeaches the witness's credibility. And we don't believe that that is a good way to proceed, and we think that it will be -- affect the fairness of the trial if, in fact, the Chamber is only admitting documents which are consistent with the witness's testimony. So our objection, in fact, is based upon the hope that the Chamber would reconsider the way it is proceeding with exhibits and allow the parties to go back to where we were by our own mutual agreement, which was to essentially have a liberal interpretation of the admission of documents. I think both sides would benefit from that, and the Chamber will benefit from that also. I know the Chamber's concerned with the number of documents that we have to deal with at the time of deliberations in the case, and it's true that that will be a burden. But, on the other hand, if we have a high bar for admissibility, it's going to really strain our resources to bring these witnesses in the Defence case to be able to make a foundation for the admissibility of these documents. In addition, I think the Prosecutor will also have to spend more resources and take more time to bring witnesses to admit documents that otherwise will fall outside of the Chamber's parameters. And in the end we think that that will actually lengthen the trial and make the process more difficult for everyone concerned. So on that basis, I would ask that you apply a rule that favours admission of documents on a more liberal basis than you did yesterday. And absent that, I propose that these 30 documents that I've identified don't meet the criteria for admission, because the witness has no personal knowledge of them and can't really speak to the document, other than the fact that they're consistent with his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, does it mean that even applying that liberal rule you referred to, these documents are not admissible; is that your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. It would be our position that these documents are admissible if you apply that liberal ruling. We would also then ask that you go back and revisit some of the documents you excluded in the previous witness. But we think that under the way we had been proceeding before yesterday, we had not planned on objecting to these documents, except for an intercepted conversation and three diaries in which the witness simply identified the handwriting. It was going to be our position that those four documents ought to be marked for identification, pending further foundation. But the rest of these documents, we had not planned on objecting to them. But when the goal-posts shifted, as it were, now we feel that these fall outside of the parameters that the Chamber set yesterday, and we're objecting on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm not prepared to speak to all aspects of what Mr. Robinson just raised, although he alluded to positions taken by the Prosecution before and, as a general matter, he mentioned a number of positions with which I don't disagree, but I would need to look a bit more carefully at all the remarks before responding. In general, I wanted to respond to the issue of the 30 documents more specifically. Again, that's not to say I take issue with Mr. Robinson's remarks; only that I'd like to take the opportunity to consider them more specifically. As a general matter, the Court is aware that the Prosecution, in the course of discussions about admissibility on previous documents, has, indeed, urged the Court to adopt a position that would result in the greatest amount of relevant information being presented to the Court. With respect to these 30 documents, it's our position that even within the guidance provided by the Chamber yesterday, these documents certainly are admissible. I would note, preliminarily, that nothing that was stated yesterday, in our judgement, was intended to or did alter the standard for admissibility of associated exhibits. In fact -- so I think we don't have a changed situation there, instead some gloss by the Court on how those guide-lines might apply to in-court submission of documents, but nothing that changed the associated exhibit standard. And when one looks more directly at that guidance, I think it's clear why these documents, these associated exhibits, are quite consistent with the guidance provided by the Court. These are precisely the opposite of the circumstances presented for most of the documents that were presented to Ms. Zaimovic. She was presented with many documents to which she responded, I have no -- I know nothing about that, they mean nothing to me, I can't tell you anything about those. Here, the situation is quite the opposite. The witness was able to illuminate the significance of those documents, explain how they were a reflection of what he observed, experienced, learned, how the document further amplifies, corroborates, or is consistent with the information he provides, how -- and the ways in which the document is accurate, and so on. I would also note that for a number of documents, the Defence suggested that the witness had not spoken to those documents. That's inaccurate. If the Court looks to, for example, the preceding or immediately subsequent paragraphs, it's very clear that the witness has incorporated the document into the information he has provided to the Court. So the out-of-context specific reference in a particular paragraph does not change the fact that the witness has, indeed, spoken to those documents and has provided the additional evidential value alluded to by Judge Morrison yesterday. So for those reasons, Your Honour, we submit that the documents are quite admissible. And should the Court not be prepared to rule on those documents immediately, the Prosecution, in the interests of time, is prepared to submit for -- a table or chart more specifically indicating what the witness said about it and how his testimony provides the additional evidential amplification to which the Court was referring yesterday and that make the documents admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Chamber will issue its decision in due course, after Judge Morrison returns. And the Chamber will try to give, as much as possible, an informed guide-line to the parties for the future conduct of the trial. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that or before we do that, there's just one other thing we'd like to raise in connection with this witness, and that is that there are three items of documents which we've either received very recently or we haven't received yet that we think are important for this witness, and they necessitate a request that we recall him. We're not making that request at this time, but I just wanted to notify you of that. And those three categories are Rule 70 material, which have just been placed in our locker last night, containing the documents authored by this witness, which we had requested earlier, and had just been released by the Rule 70 provider. And we haven't had a chance to look at those yet. Secondly, there's a series of diaries that I've been asked by Mr. Tieger to reference in private session, but I'll just say that it's 3500 pages of documents that if you want to know who the author is, we can go into private session. But we just also received those recently, and we believe they contain references to meetings that Mr. Harland's testimony and statements also refer to, and we haven't had a chance to go through those. And the last item is documents that we believe we should receive from the states pursuant to the request for binding orders dealing with violations of the UN arms embargo that could be relevant to this witness's testimony, and when the Chamber issues its decision. And if we're fortunate enough to have a positive decision and receive some more documents, those may be things we would want to visit with this witness. So I just want to make a note at this stage that there may be an application to call this witness back if things develop in that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your notice, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're going to start today the cross-examination by the Defence. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland. First of all, I would like to express my gratitude to you for your readiness to meet up with the Defence, where we managed to agree on certain matters and discuss various matters. But what I particularly appreciated was your motivation, your intention of ensuring equi-distance in view of the Prosecution and the Defence. Is that your position today as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I said, you know, I agree to participate in this process in the hope that it gets us closer to the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you something. Who held that position before you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately before me was a colleague called Emma Shitaka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I did not manage to remember you and that I cannot remember her either, but that doesn't really change the situation. Could you please tell me who held that position before she did?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because I took up the position as soon as I arrived, so I knew my immediate predecessor, but I didn't necessarily know her predecessor. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, when you came to that position, did you -- you did actually look into matters, didn't you? You wanted to see what had been done up until then; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were a lot of things going on when I arrived, so I must say there was not a lot of -- not a lot of time to do a lot of research about what had been done before in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you did familiarise yourself with everything that your superiors had signed up to, I assume.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most -- a lot of it. No, I can't say all of it, but most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us a bit about your chief mandate and what it was, and were there any other obligations involved?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal mandate or the mandate of the organisation I worked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mandate of the organisation I worked for, the mandate of UNPROFOR, was laid out in a series of Security Council resolutions, which were often not very clear because they represented a compromise between very different views about the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the -- and it's almost 20 years ago, but if I remember correctly, there's 713 is the arms embargo, I think. 817 or 81 -- no, 770 mandates UNPROFOR to protect humanitarian assistance coming into Bosnia and Herzegovina. 776 asks UNPROFOR to take certain measures to protect those convoys and Sarajevo Airport, I think. Then 817 or 819 about -- give it a particular role with respect to Srebrenica. 824 creates some safe areas. 836 authorises the use of all necessary means to deter attacks against those safe areas. So the mandate of UNPROFOR was large and complicated. My little role was to try and be the political eyes and ears for the UNPROFOR leadership in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that you focused on the political aspect rather than the military; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, though every morning I was required to sit through the briefing by the UNMOs, the United Nations Military Observers, and others, but -- and sometimes I would go to negotiations that were principally of a military character, so about cease-fires or anti-sniping agreement. But your general characterisation is correct, that the heart of my work was on the political side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a person similar to yourself on the military side, that is to say, writing up military analyses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who was probably -- had the most similar role to mine was the military assistant to the BH commander, so the military assistant then to General Briquemont and then General Rose and then General Smith. That person was usually a colonel, usually a British colonel, but it changed. I think I was the only one who stayed through most of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I got things a bit confused in that sense, mentioning Jeremy Braid, because I thought that he was doing more or less the same thing. Your joint superiors had two wings, as it were; one was political and the other was military. So you were the political assistant and there was this other military assistant; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I think if I remember -- I mean, I have only a vague -- I have a feeling that Jeremy Braid was not with UNPROFOR, because there was -- as well as UNPROFOR, which was a peacekeeping mission, there was an intergovernmental negotiation process, Lord Owen and these other characters, and they also had a political staff. My responsibilities were exclusively limited to UNPROFOR's operations in its mandated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The political aspect of these operations; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say my -- my job, when I was in BH Command, was to write the overall assessment, that is, at the end of each week, which is: What was the reporting and analysis of the mission in all its mandated areas? And those mandated areas covered a range of political factors and a range of humanitarian and military factors. But my job was to try and report on the full spectrum of them and to attempt some synthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, your colleague on the military side was involved in his own line of work, the military assistant, that is? I'm trying to say that you authored weekly political assessments, and what about him? Did he author the weekly military assessments or reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember well, but I don't think so. I don't think there was a weekly UNPROFOR military situation report from BH Command. Maybe there was, but I don't recall it, but -- and I don't recall who wrote it. But my job was to try and make a synthesis of the events that had taken place across UNPROFOR's mandated activities during the preceding seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do not have any military education, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then say this: There was UNPROFOR, whose heads had a military -- or, rather, a political assistant for political assessment, an assistant for military assessment. There were also UN military observers who had their line of reporting. There was also the European Commission and Monitoring Mission. They were completely independent from you, and they had their own line of reporting; right? And they all provided daily and weekly reports. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's generally correct. But whether our military provided a separate military report, I don't know. The way our system normally works is that at the level of the theatre headquarters, the streams of information are meant to be integrated: the political, the humanitarian, the development, the human rights, the military. And that was my particular job. It's a job that takes place in all UN peacekeeping missions, the job of trying to synthesise the different streams of information. But it's possible that what you say is correct and that there was a separate stream of purely military reporting to the military headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said that you drafted your reports based on other people's reports.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly used the information from the UNMOs and our battalions, but I also had my own office. We had, I mentioned yesterday, a medical doctor. We also had a statistician. We had political officers making meetings with people in the city and outside, and, of course, I attended directly the meetings with the leadership on both sides. I was usually sitting quietly in the background. But -- so I would say it's not correct to imply that what I had was second-hand information. There was a range of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're saying that you had a direct insight, a direct assessment, but most of your report was a compilation and analysis of other people's reports. Could you please tell us what you based your reports on? You had two types of documents, reports and political assessments, so tell us what kind of documents you produced and what they were based on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sure. So the reports on specific incidents, whether it's a meeting or something that happened to a convoy or on the battle-field, if it was at a meeting, normally I was present. Normally, I didn't say anything, but normally I was present with yourself, or President Izetbegovic, or any of the other actors, or General Mladic, or General Delic, or many others. And so normally I observed, myself. If I did not observe, myself, I had a couple of colleagues who could play the same role. In fact, I think one of them may be coming to testify later in this case. And then I would also -- for example, if it was about electricity or gas, I would also speak to the technical experts on either side, and then often the French engineers, the UNPROFOR engineers, would take me to the site and they would explain to me the problem. If it was about a military episode, sometimes the UNMOs would say what they had observed, and sometimes the French would take me in their little VBLs, their light armoured vehicles, to the site, and we would look at what occurred. So if it was reporting about a particular meeting or about a particular incident, it was normally my own observations and notes plus whatever additional material would be given to me by people who were either there or who were experts. For the weekly reporting, that was largely done on the basis of a discussion between me and those people who were providing the stream of information in, those people who were giving us the statistics on the amount of shelling, the amount of humanitarian aid coming in, the amount of sniping, or who were giving us the information on the battle-field situation, and with my superiors. And we would generally agree on how to characterise the situation. And then I was given the task of writing it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then, as we have already agreed, you synthesised all that at the end of the day; is that correct? You did it at the end of every day? And now I would --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did it at the end of every week. We would generally meet with the leadership of UNPROFOR every morning, but we would generally not attempt to make any synthesis of the situation or to make any overall analysis that we would send to Zagreb and New York. That would just be a meeting to get a factual update, on the basis of which the commander, General Briquemont or General Rose or General Smith, could give his orders for the day. It was only at the end of the week - I can't even remember now which day of the week it was - that we would try to sit together to make some synthesis of this to have a slightly bigger strategic approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that decision based on a consensus, or was there a voting process leading to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN is a difficult operating environment. It's not full, always, of like-minded people. But we managed to avoid voting on our reports. We -- but there was a sort of negotiation, I think you can say that, sometimes about how to characterise certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about UN military observers. But before that, just one more thing. Besides those meetings, and the thinking aloud, analysis, were your political assessments and reports based on some other reports, and what reports were those? What reports did you analyse in order to make your own reports through the process of synthesising those other reports?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a lot of it, we were the raw material. We were at the meeting, or our military observers were on the front-line, or our battalions were observing a change in the confrontation line, and we went to see it. There were other streams of information that needed to be included, of course, like UNHCR would give us the data every -- I can't remember, every few days or maybe once a week on where the convoys were and how many had been allowed in, and what volumes, but -- so there was a range of data, and this data became quite large, so much so that in the end we had to hire a professional statistician; in fact, I think a colleague of yours from Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask you this: Am I to conclude that if I were to participate in negotiations or, God forbid, a new war campaign, that I should pay more attention to those quiet ones sitting at the back of the room, the back-benchers; is that what you're saying? Of course, you don't want to answer the question. Tell me, what was the name of that statistician from Kosevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was -- I think it was Cavaljuga. I think. I'm not sure. Maybe, I think, Mladen -- I think Mladen Cavaljuga. But that's just one example of -- I mean, to explain how we handled large amounts of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Owing to our previous meeting, I believe that we can briefly run through a certain number of things that we already agreed on. Earlier today, you mentioned something that we already discussed and agreed on, and that was the fact that the 15 to 18 years lapsed from the events blur the memories somewhat; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements, you say that you attended about 15 meetings or so that I attended as well; for example, that you met with Koljevic and Krajisnik on a different number of occasions. But when it comes to meetings that I attended, there were 15 such occasions. Am I right? Yes, thank you. Would you please try and remember what meetings those were? Maybe you can consult your notes. What I'm interested in is what meetings you attended, yourself, and which ones were those that you had your assistant sitting in on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a series of meetings in 1990 -- in the early summer of 1993 about Igman. Unfortunately, it was always me. I didn't have any assistants. I was the assistant. Then after Igman, there were a series of meetings, almost always at this Hotel Panorama, about the withdrawal from Igman and problems that arose with that withdrawal almost from the beginning. Then there were meetings about the pre -- in 1993 about the preconditions for political negotiations on the Owen-Stoltenberg Agreement or the so-called HMS Invincible Agreement. If I remember correctly, President Izetbegovic said that he would not go to Geneva to meet with you unless something was done, and I now forget exactly the details of the "something." I think whether it was about electricity or about convoys, I can't remember. So then there may have -- there were a couple of meetings about that. Then, around the time -- in the period immediately -- so that's what I remember from 1993. There were other little meetings, too. Sometimes we would go -- on a smaller point, I would sometimes go with colleagues, sometimes Victor Andreev, the head of Civil Affairs, or someone to about some specific smaller incident which I now forget. Then in early 1994, there were the meetings around the Markale 1 incident. After the Markale 1, there was a lot of pressure from Western countries, and the question was how the Serbs would respond. Then there was, I think, a brief -- and then there were ultimatums, and weapons had to be withdrawn, and by certain dates, and so on. And then, around Gorazde, we met again. There were a series of urgent meetings. I went -- I was sitting in the room when General Rose saw you about -- at the Hotel Panorama on that occasion. I think -- I believe you were -- there were several meetings on that in April. Then I went separately with Sergio de Mello and Victor Andreev on the question of how -- whether the Serbs would be willing to withdraw from the right bank of the Drina River in Gorazde. Then there were meetings about the -- ah, yeah. No, then I had a -- because there was a Russian envoy, Mr. Churkin, and Mr. Churkin was based in Sarajevo, and he had no way to get to Pale, so I was -- in addition to my job, I was given the new and most responsible job of being his driver. And so I took him to two additional meetings also on that, and so on. So the -- the exact details and dates escape me, but this was roughly it. So either it would be Rose or Briquemont or Hayes. Ah, yeah, there was some more in 1993 with a British brigadier who was the number 2, I think, under Briquemont. There would have been one or two meetings also with him. So this is roughly -- I don't have the count now, and, in fact, if you ask me to make an exact count, I'm not sure I could, but these can be -- I guess people's diaries can be compared. I mean, I don't have the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, that won't be necessary. However, I would like to ask you this: Sometimes some of your colleagues informed you about things, for example, the investigation at Markale. So I suppose that you did not attend all the meetings. When you did not attend the meetings yourself, were you the one who drafted political assessments and a political analysis? So if you did not attend a meeting yourself, was it you who drafted them, or was it somebody else? And if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior was a Russian. And simply because he was not a native English speaker, he thought it was easier if he would just come back and tell me what had happened, and I would write very quickly a note on the basis of what he told me. So -- and, similarly, for some of the weekly reporting, he would simply tell me what had -- what had happened and what he thought the main points should be. So -- but then there -- there was, at least during one year, during -- or at least during part of one year, there was another native English speaker in the office who had a similar job to me, Tony Banbury, an American. And so, for example, there were a series of negotiations involving yourself and President Carter, and those negotiations, somehow, normally I would have gone to, but he went to. I mean, he was American, and I think he might even have known President Carter, or I can't remember now. But, anyway, he went to those meetings. So I wouldn't say that I went to all the meetings that UNPROFOR had with yourself or with even other senior members of the Serb establishment. And, similarly, sometimes the military just met by themselves with General Mladic. So I can't say that I went to all or even most of the meetings with the Serb leadership during my period, but I went to a lot of them, and maybe too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will remember that those negotiations or talks, rather, President Carter was not the opposing side, and they resulted in a four-month-long cease-fire towards the end of 1994 and the beginning of 1995; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it worked very well, but I don't think that was -- I don't think that was President Carter's fault, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. You remembered something that happened, and that was that Mr. Izetbegovic, who was the presiding of the Presidency, and I was the president of Republika Srpska, and yet you referred to him as "President," and you referred to me as "Dr. Karadzic;" is that your official position? Is that part of your doctrine? What is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is always a problem in the United Nations, what is the form of address that is used for the senior officers of a state recognised by the United Nations as a member state, versus the senior officers of political structures not represented -- not recognised as member states of the United Nations. Our position is that we are impartial, and we will discharge our mandate impartially, but that the presidents and prime ministers and senior officers of member states of the organisation do have terms of address that are reserved to themselves. I hope it doesn't compromise our impartiality, but I must say, to this day, I live with this problem with respect to, if I can say to you, the Republic of Cyprus. We would refer to President Christofias. We mean no disrespect to Mr. Talat, who is viewed in his community as, quote, "President" - or was until the election last week - viewed in his community as the president of the, quote, "Turkish Republic of North Cyprus." But after constant engagement with our lawyers and political advisors, we find it impossible, in the end, to simply treat officers of recognised member states the same as others, at least at the level of terms of address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you will agree with me, won't you -- I'm waiting for the interpretation. You will agree with me that the Serb side was one-third of the power in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm going to move on to things that we agreed on, so I would kindly ask you to just answer yes or no whenever you can. Will you agree that the Serb side that I headed, represented one-third of the state power and the state structure in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was it who represented the Serb side? What I'm talking about is the fact that we won in the elections in 1990 and we held one-third of the power. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the rump presidency, because the Presidency of Yugoslavia was referred to as a rump presidency, and your superiors also referred to the Bosnian Presidency as a rump presidency. The representatives of the Serbian people separated their sovereignty and their part of the state monopoly, and we represented that one-third that was missing from the Bosnian Presidency; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned earlier today that Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency, on the eve of all the conferences, usually gave me ultimatums that I had to meet in order for the two of us to meet in Geneva; am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said "usually," but the example I gave was certainly an example of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would quickly like to move through everything that we agreed upon when we met. In response to my question as to whether you had been warned about the possibility of cheating and deceits, your answer was, Yes, and you said that it was a shadow land; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your political assessments, your weekly political assessments, were written up by relying on military sources. The battalion reports were something that you found more useful, and that there were differences involved. First of all, can you tell me whether we have agreed on that. And, secondly, could you tell me what the differences actually were. And could you reply as briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you prefer relying on the battalion reports rather than on the military observers' reports? In my view, their main job was to observe. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should say I preferred them for different things. The UNMOs, the military observers, did some things that were very useful. They counted all of the shell fire, and they made -- they were -- and they count -- they gave statistical and quantitative data with respect to shooting. But the battalions lived and operated in particular areas of the confrontation line, and I often found that they had better depth of knowledge for just -- I'll try to be brief. But, for example, when they said they saw evidence that one side or the other was trying to prepare some military operation, my experience was that the battalion reports were more generally accurate in this regard, though they didn't count as rigorously and almost religiously the number of firings that the UNMOs did. So I used them for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the difference was not like the one in the top echelons of the UN, the one that you spoke about that was decisively impacted by the background of those coming from different countries. There was something else involved here, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, though I should say there was, in fact, sometimes a discernibly different approach from UNPROFOR units of different nationalities, depending on the way in which that country generally saw the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it is probably because of that that you established another thing, that in our situation back there, things were not always the way they seemed; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that the Muslim intention and the pattern of behaviour of the Muslim leadership was to provoke a military intervention by the West; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They openly stated that they wanted direct military support from the West, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also gave an example; namely, that the president of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic, was against having civilians leave town, and that that was motivated by political objectives. He wanted to have civilians stay there, and he wanted them to be victimised, in order to secure emotional support and military support from the West; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he -- yeah, what he -- yes. What he said to me and to others was that he did not want the civilian populations of, for example, Sarajevo or Srebrenica to be able to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will probably recall that our representatives signed, even before the war, in London, and during the war, in London again, during the Carrington Conference, an agreement on freedom of movement on the part of civilians. Have you heard of that agreement? It was signed in the summer of 1992, but you probably had insight into what you had inherited, as it were.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, may I ask one question. Did he give you a reason why he didn't want the population to leave at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was speaking to him, I believe he said -- I asked him about his decision to block -- in 1993, he had instructed UNHCR -- he had told UNHCR that he would not accept the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica at a time when there was great difficulty in Srebrenica. And when I asked him about that, he said that it would be giving in to ethnic cleansing, so it would be giving that territory which previously had a Bosniak majority. It would be giving that territory to the Serbs. So he thought that the -- he thought that the people should stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the question of Dr. Karadzic to you, he asked whether he wanted the civilian population to be victimised. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't sure that it was useful to speculate as to people's deeper motivations. There was certainly -- there was certainly people who believed that the West, NATO, would not intervene unless they saw the situation as being particularly dire, particularly difficult. So there were certainly those who believed that, among other things, having the civilian population basically present on the battle-field would make it more likely that Western nations would be shocked into wanting to intervene militarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I could agree with you that Mr. Izetbegovic tried, by keeping civilians in Srebrenica, to keep Srebrenica in military terms, although he could do that on the basis of the Agreement on Safe Havens. But I believe you will recall that General Morillon kept trying to obtain our agreement to have the civilians from Srebrenica evacuated to Tuzla. Do you remember that? There are a lot of documents attesting to that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was happening just before I arrived. So I spoke to General Morillon about it, but I was not in the country during the events of April 1993, which I think you are describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. But after that, up until 1995, someone kept asking him to ask us to give our approval for the transfer of civilians from Srebrenica to Tuzla, and in return we asked him to make it possible to have Serbs evacuated from Tuzla. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we're going to use other documents. However, what I asked about civilians primarily pertained to Sarajevo. So Mr. Izetbegovic, as we have agreed, was against having civilians leave Sarajevo. Yesterday, with the previous witness, we discussed this and saw that renowned physicians were sentenced to 28 and 32 months in prison because of their attempts to leave Sarajevo. What do you think was the reason why Mr. Izetbegovic did not allow people to leave Sarajevo? Of course, criminals were very happy to see that, because they made people pay money in order to cross the lines. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to speculate on his motivation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no speculation, no speculation. But we have agreed that he was against having civilians leave town; right? I mean Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I believe there were -- you needed a formal -- if you wanted to leave the city, you needed to get some sort of formal document. So I think it was not simply my reporting; I think it was an established fact known to everybody. I think if you tried to leave the city without this, you could be in grave danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what their state authorities did; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, if I remember correctly, you needed a document, a permission, to get out of the city if you wanted to leave. For example, when there were buses with little NGOs that were allowed through, I mean, I remember the one, the Children's Embassy, if you wanted to get on that bus, you needed clearances from, I think, from both the Bosnian Army and from the civilian authorities, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that you were aware of the fact that at the time, the Serbs had agreed to the Muslims having their own territories in the Drina River Valley; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that re-arming had taken place in protected areas, and that Mr. Izetbegovic actually confirmed that to you after the war, when you were compiling reports on the fall of Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe he even said that in his own book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, and I believe that we are going to tender that during this examination, he told you that he never wanted to exchange Srebrenica, because he had wanted to do that, he would not have sent sophisticated weapons there, physicians, helicopters, et cetera. On one occasion, one of the helicopters was downed, three physicians were killed, and there were sophisticated weapons there. He said that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe he also again said that in his book when he is quoting his interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that one of your co-workers was involved in the Markale investigation, and you said that you did not take part in this investigation and that you were not at Markale when what happened did happen; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to remind you of some very important things that you said on many occasions. You said, in General Milosevic's trial, in Dragomir Milosevic's trial, ID 98-29, transcript dated the 15th of January, 2007, that is, on page 395, you said that if it were possible to observe sniper action at Grbavica, it would be evident that Muslims, Bosnians -- we're Bosnians, too, but, okay, the Muslims, used sniper fire against the civilians, perhaps more than the Serbs, taking into account sniper victims and sniper shooting in the area that was under the control of the Muslim government; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that there were maybe even more sniper victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, then I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "When it had been possible to monitor sniping in Grbavica, it appeared that the Bosnians were sniping at civilians probably more than the Serbs, based on counting sniper rounds and sniper victims in areas controlled by the Bosnian government."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, we did keep -- our UNMOs kept statistics, and our battalions, on the number of sniper rounds, so that may be statistically correct with respect to that area, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the preceding against President Milosevic in 2003, transcript page 28684, you said: [In English] "In late summer 1994, to the extent that the UN could monitor sniper activity in Grbavica, it appeared that the Muslims were sniping more civilians than the Serbs." [Interpretation] Isn't that right? That's what you stated; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the trial of President Milosevic, on the 5th of November, 2003, on page 286797 [as interpreted], you said: [In English] "In meetings in Grbavica, the Serbs would often complain that they were suffering from sniping from the Bosniaks." [Interpretation] Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement dated the 4th of September, 2009 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My apologies, but page 286797 actually doesn't exist in the Milosevic transcript. Maybe there's one number off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably. He can correct the number. What page did you refer to? November 2003 evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28679, probably. There is an extra "7" that is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope you can locate the part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whenever it is convenient, you can take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On that page reference number, with Mr. Sladojevic's help, we found that it's 28697, and that refers to the page of the transcript in the trial of -- in the Milosevic case mentioned at page 29 of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, for the sake of the participants in these proceedings, we would like to show a map now. We talked about Grbavica, and I would ask you to mark Grbavica, the parts of town that were held by the Serbs, city proper. 1D790. Could I have that map, please. 11790 [as interpreted]. I think it is a satellite image rather than a map. Thank you. Could Mr. Harland please be given a pen, an electronic pen. I think that should be it, yes. I would like to ask you whether you see a red line and a blue line here, and I'm asking you whether these are the lines of separation, or the front-line, or whether this is the area of Sarajevo in general.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and yes. So red is the Serb forward positions, blue is the Bosniak forward positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now please mark Grbavica that we discussed in relation to Muslim sniping, Muslim sniping at Grbavica. So could you please mark Grbavica now.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see it, but I think that you've marked Vrace. Grbavica is further down.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please mark Iradramsko Naselje [phoen] near Dobrinja. That's an area in the south-west of Dobrinja that we held.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've never been very good at maps, but maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, yes. Could you please put little Xs or crosses or something. Could you please mark Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put initials, so for the future reference, "G" for Grbavica, "D," and "N," or something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can write.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now mark the eastern part of Dobrinja. We controlled some of the buildings in that area. Could you please just put a little cross or a letter D?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that would be here or here, yeah. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There as well, yes, thank you. Could you please put an "I" next to the Serbian part of Ilidza within the red front-lines. It's the western-most part of that map.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right there. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely. And now could you please mark Hrasnica. That's an area within the Muslim lines, south of the runway. In depth towards Mount Igman and adjacent to the runway is Butmir, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Butmir, yes. So Butmir is here somewhere, yeah. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And south of that is Hrasnica, it continues?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think barely on this map, maybe. I'm not sure. Here, maybe. I'm not sure. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now west or, rather, left of Butmir is the so-called Sokolovic colony; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Somewhere here. I don't know. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Thank you. I think that you can sign this map. But before that, can we please look at Vogosca. It is not clearly visible, but it's in the north up on the map; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think somewhere up there, I think. Yeah. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And below this initial, can you see that the front-line goes through Vogosca, itself, Gornji Hotonj, Donji Hotonj, and Kobilja Glava, and Ogorsko [phoen] as Muslim villages are under the Muslim control; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we going west from my V or east from my V?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: South.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: South, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I forget which one was which, but, you know, Kobilja Glava, somewhere in here, these places. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that what you have just marked is Zuc. But next to the red line is a blue line in the city, about a centimetre and a half below your initial V.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, uh-huh. Okay. So right here, yeah. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, yes. Thank you. And can we now identify which parts of the city proper are controlled by the Serbs? Grbavica is a neighbourhood with large blocks of buildings, and the same is true of the adjacent area; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about parts of Dobrinja and the airport and neighbourhood? The height of the buildings there is the same as the height of the buildings in the adjacent neighbourhoods; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please ask you to mark Mojmilo? I believe that it is clearly visible above Dobrinja. I'm sure that you're familiar with the area. Can you just put an M?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it there? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're sure, yes, of course, that's it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I was never very good a geography, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Nedzarici was an area of residential buildings not more than one or two storeys high at the most?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was a 100 per cent Serb settlement; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was -- that was the case when I was there. Whether that was the case before, I'm not entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The Serbs moved into the city by setting up Nedzarici. Do you agree that Alipasino Polje and whatever the neighbours of the neighbourhoods are called adjacent to Nedzarici, and those neighbourhoods north-east of Nedzarici, mostly consisted of high-rise buildings or blocks of buildings? Do you agree? Those are high-rise buildings, blocks of buildings, modern buildings; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for the record, is it the place where you marked as A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one, Alipasina Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you read the transcript later on, it's very difficult to find where it is. Thank you. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you put a Z next to the place where you identified Zuc?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this high ground somewhere, yeah, somewhere in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a bit more to the west. The first cross that you placed on the map, I believe that that's Zuc.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you identify whom for us, whom village with the relay -- this is an isolated hilltop across from Alipasina Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I looked at it every day on the map, the tower with the bulb. But where it is exactly on the map, I don't know. It might be this one. [Marks] I'm not sure. It's one of those hills to the north of the main down-town area, but exactly which hills, I'm not sure I can easily mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could circle it in order to distinguish --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not sure whether I -- I'm not sure whether I'm passing my geography test. I'm not sure whether I have, in fact, placed my H on the hill that was precisely --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Yes, that is Hum, right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark Sokolje and the part above Rajlovac. Do you know where Rajlovac is? In the very west, in the left.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here [indicates], yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, quite a bit more south, and the hilltop is above Rajlovac itself. Can you see that? I believe that you marked Mr. Krajisnik's village, and you can see the urban part of Rajlovac next to the border of the map, southward, next to the border, close to the margin.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. [Indicates] Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Is the hilltop above Rajlovac known as Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates] This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A bit more to the east, at the very top, the very summit.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I'm -- yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's where your radar was; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, yes. We had one radar position there at one point, and then another radar position, I think, near the -- exactly at the opposite end of the town. Earlier, we had, I think, also a mortar-detecting radar on Zuc and Hum, but I think they came to a bad end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now above the S, where the radar position was, could you put an R or a circle or a triangle to mark the radar position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe somewhere here. [Marks] I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was at the very top, which was a bit more south. I believe that you marked it as if it had been in the valley, and that's --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a bad place for a radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And can we now move on towards the old part of the city. Can you see Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Grdonj is in the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is. But can you see the Jajce barracks in this map?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the slope somewhere here at the far eastern end of the city. Just one second. I forget now which one is Jajce barracks, which one is Turkish Fort. Shall I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I put a J for Jajce barracks there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now if you move towards the western part of the map, so in the left-side direction, would that be the Grdonj hilltop?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: West of -- north-west of Jajce barracks, yeah, maybe. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes -- the promontory, the hill top that you see, the lighter colour. Is that Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be there, yeah. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But that's still within the Muslim lines, a little bit below the blue line; right? You marked the village of Mrkovici. However, the lighter area depicting the summit, that's Grdonj Hill; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's no doubt about the fact that Grdonj was under Muslim control; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we now move into the southern part of the city east of Grbavica. There are some hilltops there. Do you know where Colina Kapa is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one I visited there was Debelo Brdo, but I'm not sure I can exactly say which one it is there. You mean, you know, next to Grbavica, yeah, just east of Grbavica, yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the north-east of Grbavica. The first one is Debelo Brdo, and the next one is Colina Kapa within the blue lines. They held both Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now between Mojmilo and Vrace, can you see the ridge? That's Hrasno Brdo; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere in here above the little settlement of Hrasno, yeah. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm talking about the ridge from M, south of the H that you marked, all the way up to the Vrace, and the line -- the distance between the blue and the red line is about 20 to 50 metres [realtime transcript read in error "250"], not more than that; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly looks close.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that east of the letter H that you marked -- in the transcript, it says "250," and it should read "between 20 and 50 metres." Do you agree, Mr. Harland, that where the lines are the closest east of H, that that is Ozrenska Street, and that in Ozrenska Street, the Muslims were on one side of the streets and the Serbs were on the other side of the street? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are talking about H in the middle of this map. We have three Hs in this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can remember exactly where the line ran in that point, but certainly there were places where the line ran down the middle of streets, or sometimes even where it went through buildings. There's one building, I think, near -- well, a little north-east of there, I think, where it even cut through some buildings. But the general point is certainly correct, that the lines were extremely close in that southern portion of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the northern hilly part, the distance was between 230 and 300 metres, but here in the south, the distance was anything between 20 and 50 metres, not more than that. I'm talking now about the southern part of the city.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Can we now agree about a number of issues? First of all, did Muslims hold Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I arrived, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they also hold the ridge north-east of Mojmilo, the ridge known as Hrasno Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they hold Sokolje, the area in the very east of the map where your radar position had been or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: West --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the west, in the west, above Rajlovac. Did they hold the entire mountain range over there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Sokolje was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they hold Hum?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they hold Zuc Hill? By the time you arrived, we had already lost it. We had controlled it before you came; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they hold Grdonj, in the very north, above the old city?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sedonj [phoen], Grdonj, and so on and so forth. They also held the Jajce barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that they held Debelo Brdo, Colina Kapa, and those trig points on the slopes of Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that Debelo Brdo was contested, but it may be correct as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that those positions of the Muslim Army were dominant with regard to the neighbouring villages populated by the Serbs? In other words, they were on the hilltops and we were in the valleys. Look at the map and it will become clear. Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the narrowest sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the narrowest and broader sense, all Serbs around Mojmilo were in an inferior position, as it were, and the same applies to Sokolje; right? The Serbs were in an inferior position with regard to the positions of the Muslim Army; right? Was Rajlovac inferior in contrast to Sokolje? I mean, it's clear on the map, in geographical terms; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think it's representative of the broader picture, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Nedzarici inferior with regard to Mojmilo and at the high-rise buildings in the neighbouring Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the airport settlements and the eastern part of Dobrinja? Would you say that the Serbs were inferior with regard to Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now what about Vogosca; was it inferior vis-a-vis Zuc and the neighbouring Muslim positions, just as Grbavica was inferior with regard to Zuc and Hum?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies again, and it may be just me, but perhaps I could ask for some clarification. I'm unsure what Dr. Karadzic means by his use of the word "inferior" in these repeated questions. I see Mr. Harland might have some understanding of it, by his answers, but I'm unsure what he means by the word "inferior." Inferior in what regard, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He has been able to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, actually, I would be keen to comment, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the point of these dozens of questions is to give the general impression that the Serb communities, geographically, were tactically inferior or tactically more exposed, then I think it's basically an inversion of the reality. The basic reality is that hundreds of thousands of people in the valley of the city [marks], which is where most of the people lived, were right on the floor of the valley, very exposed to Serb fire. And I think narrowly and factually, Dr. Karadzic is right, as we go around from one little specific example to another, that he has found a Serb community that is at a tactical disadvantage because it is at a lower elevation from a Bosnian-government-held hill or tall building, but it's not at all representative of what was going on in the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You already said it was not representative of a bigger picture earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the intervention on the part of my learned friend from the Prosecution should have been part of re-examination. It was not an objection. I wanted to assist Mr. Harland in expressing himself. I wanted to hear from him whether there were places where they were in an inferior position, and there were also places where we were in an inferior position. Was that recorded? I don't think that your answer has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that all Serb neighbourhoods had a hilltop or two towering above them and held by the Muslim Army? I can name them for you, if that's of any assistance. Grbavica, Nedzarici, the airport settlement, Dobrinja 1 and 4. I don't know which one we held. In the east, in any case. Rajlovac, Ilidza, Gornji Kotorac, Lukavica. Could you please mark Lukavica for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, God, I thought I had escaped my geography lesson. Is it somewhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: East -- [overlapping speakers]. No, no, I believe that what you're marking now is Gornji Kotorac. Lukavica is east of D1 and 2, east of Dobrinja. Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go as far as Kasindol or somewhere, but here, I don't know. Lukavica [marks] --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. I believe that what you're showing now is Tilava, and Lukavica is between L and D; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps. But to answer your question, I would say that certainly as you walked or drove around Serb areas, Serb-held areas of Sarajevo, like Ilidza, you felt much less exposed to fire than almost anywhere on the inside of the confrontation line. But you are certainly right that there were communities very close to the confrontation line that were exposed to fire and felt very dangerous, like Dobrinja and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please make an arrow pointing from Hrasnica towards Igman. Igman towers above Hrasnica in the entire southern area; right? It's a dominant position.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below our map, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We'll see that later. And now could you please answer this: The Serb part of Vogosca, which is below Zuc, Hotonj, and Kobilja Glava, was it tactically inferior vis-a-vis Muslim position? And what about Rajlovac vis-a-vis Sokolje, was Serbian Ilidza tactically inferior with Mojmilo and Igman? And Nedjarici, was it tactically inferior vis-a-vis Mojmilo, the high-rise buildings in Igman? And then the airport settlement, the part of Dobrinja held by Serbs, Lukavica, Tilava, and Kasima [phoen], were all those inferior vis-a-vis to Igman? If you held Igman, could you actually shell all those areas as you will, whenever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you had weapons to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will we agree that Grbavica could be targeted from Grdonj, Zuc, Hum, and from the city, from anywhere in the city, from Hrasno, for example, from Pofalici, and so on and so forth? Was Grbavica at a tactical disadvantage vis-a-vis Debelo Brdo, Colina Kapa? Could Grbavica be targeted from by many dominant positions which were held by the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the floor of the valley of Sarajevo. And like other places on the floor of the valley of Sarajevo, most of them Bosnian-government-held, it was rather exposed, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please initial this, and I would like to tender this map into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before we keep it, could you mark -- add "1" to one of the Ls which you erroneously marked as Lukavica for identification purpose, a "1."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure we've ever perfectly identified the real Lukavica in here, but it's certainly somewhere in there. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to add "1" to the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So add "1," all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then could you put the date of today. So it is the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Edgerton, I'm concerned about reading this part of the transcript later on, again. So I wonder whether you can sit down with either Mr. Robinson or Mr. Sladojevic, with the assistance of the mapping unit, whether you can put all the full names of these places into this map. So we'll mark and keep this map separately, but think about whether you can produce a map, with the assistance of the Map Unit, with the full names of these locations discussed today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I may, this -- the base map of this satellite map, and I'm sure Your Honours are probably already aware, but for the record is Map number 2 in the Prosecution's map book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have it. And then if you can produce while the witness is here, then you can get the confirmation from Mr. Harland as well. It's for you. Let's proceed. Yes, we can admit this map as marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map marked -- the marked map will be Exhibit D134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, now I'd like to remind you of what you said in your statement of the 4th of September, 2009. 066-9895, up until 9984, and then on page 66-9918, or, rather, 81. And I would also like to remind you of what you said in the Dragomir Milosevic trial. Actually, it has to do with the same number. It's the same -- the transcript reference is the 16th of -- 19th of January, page 405. This is what I'm referring to. You said that you were aware of two incidents: [In English] "... one in late 1893 [sic] and one in early 1994 of Bosniak snipers shooting at Bosniaks, including one where General Rose's bodyguard returned fire at the Bosniaks shooting at the Bosniaks." [Interpretation] Is that right, is that what you said?
