utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if I said that, but I do remember the two incidents that are referred to there. So it's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in General Milosevic's trial, on the 16th of January, 2007, transcript page 405 through 407, you asserted the following: [In English] "... that there was a victim of shelling or sniping on Bosnian-controlled territory. It was assumed in the international media that the firing had been from the RS Army territory." [Interpretation] Is that right that these were assessments from the media?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then again the Dragomir Milosevic trial, the 16th of January, 2007, the same page numbers, 405 through 407, this is what you said. You said that you were: [In English] "... aware of any instance whether the Republika Srpska Army shot at their own civilians and doubted if there was any such instance. This was separate to any incident where one Serb group might have been conflicting with another or a Serb might have killed another Serb due to criminal or political differences." [Interpretation] Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it sounds correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this one, I feel I have to rise. Without reference to the line numbers, I found what I think is the passage that Dr. Karadzic is referring to. And while I accept there might be some variation in translation, it might be preferable to work off the actual transcript, and that's not what the transcript that I have in front of me records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with what Mr. Karadzic referred to is only four or five lines, but he referred to three pages. And so could you check the reference again, whether it is correct, and then whether what you read out, is it a correct reflection of that part of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 406. It's that transcript, page 406, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Harland said he can't remember, but it sounds correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then in your statement of the 4th of September, 2009, 066-9895, up until 9984, on page 66-9932, you said -- you established that there was an anti-sniping agreement. Now I'd like to ask you about something that you had said. You said that with regard to the anti-sniping agreement, the leadership had more success in preventing sniper activity than in terms of orders outside the sniping agreement. Is that right? That's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If that's what Mr. Harland said yesterday, please could we be assisted by at least a page reference from yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to find it now. I was taking notes. I didn't look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the essence was that you said that the leadership could prevent things, but that they were not successful outside the anti-sniping agreement. However, your proof of this is that for a while, while there was an anti-sniping agreement, there was some success; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what I said, I can't remember. But my position is that there was a substantial reduction in sniper fire after the signature of the anti-sniping agreement. We could count fewer shots and fewer victims after that agreement was signed. And to us, that was indicative of a degree of effective command and control over this by both sides. I hope I said the same thing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to put another possibility to you as well. If I issue an order for sniping to stop and that is not within the agreement, do you agree that it is more difficult for my army to stop if the other side doesn't stop as well? I mean, if the other side is shooting, how can my unilateral order be successful, or it simply cannot be as successful as it would be in the case if the other side stopped as well? I would like to have an audible answer for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in General Milosevic's trial, in the transcript on the 15th of January, 2007 - 335 is the page reference, 336 as well - you said: [In English] "... the agreement was intended to limit sniping against civilians, but also that might be called legitimate military sniping between the opposing forces, since the UN believed that the two could not be distinguished properly." [Interpretation] Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently. Yes, that is my position. I can't remember whether I said exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that because many soldiers waged war wearing civilian clothes? You, or rather the UN, had this dilemma as to distinguishing between civilians and the military. Was that, for instance, because 75 per cent of the Bosnian Army did not have uniforms? That is based on their sources. Is that the reason why you had that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was the reason? [In English] "... could not be distinguished properly."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I visited sniper positions either on the Bosnian side or on the Serb side, they, themselves, were normally trying to avoid getting shot at, so normal -- they might make a small hole in a wall, and sometimes they would even make another hole in a wall behind, and then they would rest their rifle. So they have an extremely narrow view of fire. That was true for Bosnian sniper positions and for Serb sniper positions that I saw. But the same snipers would move from one nest like this to another, sometimes even after a few minutes, it seemed. And sometimes the alignment of their line of sight was onto an area where civilians might pass. Sometimes they were firing against other snipers. Sometimes they were firing against trench lines. But it was the same people, with the same weapons, doing the same jobs from the same set of many positions, so our view was that it was extremely difficult to stop one type of this activity if you didn't just tell them all to stop -- give them all an order on both sides to stop their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember that sniper shooters also availed themselves of empty buildings, especially government buildings, so they would move in depth so as not to be exposed, whereas they had a clear line of sight?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it was hard to eliminate that by other snipers; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in your statement of the 10th of February, 1998 - 005-8216 up until 005-8243, but this is on page 58226 - this is from the Milosevic case as well, the transcript is from the 15th of January, 2007, on pages 394 through 396, this is what you said: [In English] "The background of this anti-sniping agreement, the sniping of Serb civilians by the Bosniaks which had been partly behind the closure of the blue routes, there had been a number of particularly nasty incidents, including one notorious episode where two young Serb girls were killed by a sniper who had apparently boasted that he had waited until they were properly aligned -- perfectly aligned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise again for perhaps my own confusion, but I don't see that, those words, anywhere in the transcript. Is Dr. Karadzic quoting from his statement or from the transcript? Just to have this precision, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have to be very precise as to the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the essence of what Mr. Harland said on those two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right? Do you agree? And in the statement, I mean. Do you agree, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. When you put to the witness about what he said, you have to be precise, without paraphrasing them. If you are going to paraphrase, you have to say that it is paraphrased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can comment that it is a generally correct characterisation. I cannot remember what I said in the 1998 statement, which was 12 years ago, of course, or even exactly what I said in the trial, but the general characterisation is correct, and there was -- I know the -- remember the specific incident about these two Serb girls, I think, and I think it was actually the beginning of 1995. But I can't remember exactly what was said by me in which statement or whatever. But the general characterisation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, one just technical advice. When you change your language and when you start reading out in English, you need to put a short pause for the benefit of the interpreters and court reporters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do apologise for this lack of precision in respect to the transcript. However, what Mr. Harland confirmed is on page 11 of the statement from 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those two girls were killed with a single bullet, and he waited for them to be properly aligned so that he could shoot them with one bullet; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic - the transcript reference is from the 5th of November, 2003 - on page 28684 you stated, and now I'd like to read it in English: [In English] "During late summer 1994, to the extent that the UN could monitor sniper activity in Grbavica, it appears that the Muslims were sniping more civilians than the Serbs." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I said exactly that, but I believe that is what the statistics for the Grbavica area said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more example in relation to snipers. In your statement of the 10th of February, 1998, pages 005-8216 up until 005-8243, on page 58266 -- or, rather, 226, sorry, and also in the proceedings against Dragomir Milosevic, General Milosevic, or, rather, nine years later on the 15th of January, 2007, on page 397, and on the 16th of January, on 458 page, this is what you said: [In English] "The French were sometimes unsure if long-distance shots at Bosniak civilians occasionally came from the Bosniaks rather than the Serbs." [Interpretation] Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there might be a mistake in the translation, uh-huh, or -- what is this -- how does the sentence begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm really quite lost as to where this quotation comes from. Please. I don't see it on page 458 of the transcript in the Dragomir Milosevic case. I don't see it on page 397 of the transcript. If we could just have some guidance, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I really don't know how can I help you out. But, Mr. Karadzic, please be precise in the future in references. Let's move on, and find out the precise page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 397, and now I'm going to tell you what the lines are. Between 1 and 13, in that area. Have we found it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've found something, and I appreciate that, Dr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Could you put your question again. Mr. Harland didn't understand what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on these two or three occasions, you said that the French were sometimes unsure as to who was shooting at Muslim civilians, was it the Bosniaks or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to draw your attention to the transcript of the 5th of November, 2003, in President Milosevic's trial. 28699 is the page reference. And you said something similar in the transcript in the proceedings against General Dragomir Milosevic the 16th of January, 2007. The page reference is 444. I'm going to quote it, but the essence is, and now I am going to speak in English -- I'll paraphrase, rather: [In English] "It was more common in Sarajevo for the Muslims to launch an attack in order to provoke a response from the Serbs." [Interpretation] And now comes the quotation: [In English] "They wanted the media to see the Serbs attacking and thought they had to sometimes create the conditions for that." [Interpretation] Now I'm paraphrasing: [In English] "The media was not present in other parts of the country, so the Muslims would have less incentive to do that." [Interpretation] Probably in other areas. I mean, the second part is paraphrased, and it's from President Milosevic's trial, the transcript of the 7th of November, 2003, page 28699. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I -- but the overwhelming volume of fire into Sarajevo came from the Serb side. But in some cases, it did not, and in some cases, we could not determine. But these specific quotes, I cannot anymore exactly confirm, but the general characterisation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The emphasis here is on the media and on the Muslim need to engage in provocations where the media were, not in other parts of the country where there were no media; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the media was a key factor in the strategy of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Now I would like us to recall what you stated earlier on, and primarily what we agreed upon the other day. You said that you felt that Sarajevo was under siege; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sarajevo was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then I told you that a lieutenant colonel told you that Sarajevo was not under siege, but rather within a military encirclement; right? Lieutenant Fuhrer -- Fuhrer, yeah?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I remember our conversation on Monday correctly, I said that there had been a siege of Sarajevo. You asked me whether I was aware that Colonel Fuhrer had said that he would not characterise it as a siege, he would characterise it as a military encirclement. And I said I felt that was a little pedantic. Nobody denied that the siege of Leningrad was a siege, even though the Soviet forces were able to move some tiny amount of material, some small amount of material over Lake Lagoda. So, I mean, I don't want to get into a debate about what we said to each other on Monday. But, roughly, my position has been, at the level of common sense, there was a siege of Sarajevo, and the vast majority of victims were the victims of fire coming in from the Serb side, but that there was some uncertainty about some cases. I hope that's what I conveyed to you on Monday, and it's certainly a view I have long held. But I met Colonel Fuhrer, and I respect his opinion as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you try and remember how many times Hitler approved those transports across Lagoda Lake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not relevant. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, if Leningrad has been mentioned and put within the context of Sarajevo, I'm putting it to Mr. Harland that Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You stated -- or, rather, we agreed, the two of us -- or, rather, your position was that the Army of Republika Srpska did allow water, gas, and electricity to reach Sarajevo, but it was not an act of mercy, but an act of interest, because there were a number of Serbs living there, between 20.000 to 50.000, and then your conclusion was they needed each other.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right? Is that correct? That was the question. Is that what you said, and did we agree to agree on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps Mr. Sladojevic or Ms. Edgerton will correct me, but as I recall our conversation on Monday, I said that -- you said that if it had not been for the Serbs, the Muslims would have had nothing but air; they had no springs of water or sources of electricity or gas. I said it's not quite true they had no water. They had some control of water at, I think, Lapisnica and Mostanica, and that it's true that much of the water and gas and electricity came from the Serb side of the line. But I don't think I said it was because of this population of 20.000 to 50.000 in -- Serbs in the Bosnian-government-controlled territory. I believe, perhaps those who were there can confirm, that I said it was because Serb communities, such as Ilidza and Grbavica, which were controlled by the Serb forces, also needed the water and electricity and gas that was coming into the district. So there was an interest on both sides, the Bosnian government side and on the Serb side, and so I said I did not feel that the Serbs had provided any -- the small amount of water and gas and electricity that got through as an act of charity, but as an act of interest, and this is what created the negotiations. But I think I'm right about what we talked about on Monday, but there are others in this room who can confirm it if there is a disagreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did say that. You did say that ones depended on the others, and if the Serbs had closed things on the one side, the Muslims would have done it on the other side. That's how they depended on each other, that's how they needed each other. That's your sentence. I'm quoting you. "They needed each other."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that we agreed that in the zone of Sarajevo, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, its 1st Corps, had a large numerical advantage with regard to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or, rather, the Serb Army. This means that the Muslim Army had anything between 30.000 and 50.000, at least on paper 50.000, whereas the Serbs had about 17.000; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, you asked me whether I knew how many people were serving in the 1st Corps of the armija, the Bosnian Armija, and I guessed that it was up to about 50.000, at least on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had about 17.000 troops?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we had to guess, and we guessed that it had about 20.000 on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we agreed that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had to defend its zone from attacks coming from town and those coming from Central Bosnia, that anything between 17.000 to 20.000 men had to defend themselves from the 1st Corps, which was in town, and also from the attacks from the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Corps that attacked from the areas where Serbs were dominant?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked that question, and I agreed that was correct. But you didn't ask the next question, which was: Were all of the members of the Bosnian Army 1st Corps within the area that was encircled by the Serbs? In fact, I think that just as the Sarajevo Romanija Corps of the Serb Army had other military problems, other than the siege of Sarajevo, that is also true of the Bosnian Army 1st Corps, which used to rotate large units of troops, many of them, through the tunnel out into other areas that were within the area of responsibility of 1st Corps through this Igman zone that you will recall and into many other areas. So broadly speaking, your characterisation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more question before the break. Am I right? Are you planning our next break any time now? It seems that we also agreed that every neighbourhood, at the very beginning of the conflict, which means on the 5th or 6th of April, 1992, that those neighbourhoods created front-lines which more or less did not change up until the end of the war; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember we had a discussion in which you pointed out that the communities that had been dominantly Serb prior to the war were then controlled by the Serbs during the war, and the communities that were dominantly Bosniak were generally controlled by the Bosniaks. And I pointed out that there were -- the great majority of the urban area of Sarajevo was somewhat ethnically mixed. So we had a long discussion on that, but the general characterisation that the front-lines, as they came to be shaped, did emerge from the dynamics that you described, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will be talking about those settlements. We have a map that I already showed you, but, yes, I agree that we agreed on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before we break, I wanted to indicate that, as I mentioned this morning, since we received Mr. Robinson's list of challenged documents last night, we began preparing a short chart in order to -- so as not to take valuable court time, indicating a response to the objections document by document, so we'll be submitting those electronically at the break to the Chamber and the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's continue. We, with the indulgence of the interpreters, reporters, all the staff, we will continue until 2.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I have just one minute at the very conclusion of the session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And on Monday, as I indicated, we'll have an extended sitting. We'll have four times one-and-a-half-hour sessions, starting from 9.00, and we'll have a break at 10.30. The next session will start at 11.00, continuing to 12.30, and we'll have a one-hour break, and then we'll have another two one-and-a-half-hour sessions from then. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I'll try not to quote, but to face you with some of the positions that you advocated, and then we shall see whether we will agree or not. If we don't, I'll have to accept that. But I believe that we will agree. Do you remember that your position was that some Muslim officials or leaders believed that the worse it was, the better it was, and they tried to portray the sufferings of their own people in Sarajevo as being even bigger and more substantial than it was in order to provoke the Western intervention? Was that your position? Is that what you stated at one point?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my position, yes, that the Bosnian government tended to try to overstate the suffering of the population, while the Serbs tried to understate it. Yes, I would say that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that the Bosnian government refused to reopen gas lines, even when the Serbs agreed to that, or allegedly caused outages by shelling electrical production facilities, or transformers, or whatever they're called, or, rather, high-voltage lines, and they would snipe those in order to break the electricity supply. Did you confirm that; did you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the gas, yes, there were occasions of that. With the electricity, I don't think on the generators or the transformer stations. But, yes, I am aware that there were cases when they were shooting at the insulators on the electrical lines from the Bosnian side of the line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw a document in this courtroom when Ambassador Okun was here. Shall I maybe bring it up? The document says that Mr. Cuny, or Cony -- did you know Mr. --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fred Cuny, yeah, who died in Chechnya.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He wrote Morton Abramowitz about an astonishing discovery, and that was that the Serbs enabled the repair of water lines. He invited the government to open those. The government didn't want to do that. They did it of their own will, without asking them. And then the government officials came and closed it. And then he described how, after that, water was being sold on the black market, and so on and so forth. Are you familiar with that case?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember he was very involved in trying to increase the flow of water at Lapisnica, yeah, and there were a lot of obstacles he encountered from the government side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also maintain a position that the Serbs, or perhaps Muslims and Croats who -- or even Muslims and Croats who found themselves in the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo and wanted to leave, would not be allowed to do that, the Muslim authorities would forbid them to do that, and that was another violation of human rights?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience was they didn't allow any civilians to leave, except in exceptional circumstances. But the decision was generally not based on whether they were Bosniak or Serb or Croat. They wanted all the civilians to stay, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, at the time when you stated that, your position was that that was a violation of human rights, the rights of civilians to free movement; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding as a non-lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated that you had met with such a position on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic, vis-a-vis to Sarajevo, vis-a-vis to Srebrenica; the position was equal, despite the level of danger and threat that the civilians were exposed to and despite their desire to change their places of residence; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, President Izetbegovic was very clear that he would not give permission to the civilian population to leave, even if they wanted to escape from areas of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, when we're talking about General Morillon, that local authorities pleaded with General Morillon to take their civilians out so as they could fight more freely? Let me jog your memory. There was such a case in Besici, and there's a case like that in Podrinje. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "the local authorities," you mean the Bosniak local authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and the military commanders as well. They wanted the civilians to leave. There was a case like that in Kotor Varos, in Vecici, Siprage, and then along the Drina River. And General Morillon was under a lot of pressure. We would have allowed that under the condition that he also took Serbs out of Tuzla. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was before my time, but I certainly can confirm that it was the position of President Izetbegovic that the civilian population should stay in Srebrenica even though there had been trucks organised between UNHCR and the local authorities to evacuate them. But he did confirm that they would not be allowed to enter Bosnian-government controlled territory around Tuzla, so that's what I remember from the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you saw a letter written, by Mr. Izetbegovic and sent to the United Nations, to that effect about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From 1993, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He wrote to the Secretary-General about his report about Srebrenica, and you saw the letter; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether it was to the Secretary-General or to the UN High Commission for Refugees. I originally saw the letter, in fact, in the archives of UNHCR in Geneva, which they gave me access to when I was doing some research about Srebrenica some years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you were in a position to confirm Izetbegovic's requests for thousands of tons of ammunition and weapons that had passed through the Sarajevo tunnel, and that that tunnel was used to support the black market or -- the black market while Sarajevo was either encircled or besieged; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly confirm that weapons and ammunition and many other goods came through the tunnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that you also established that when you arrived in Sarajevo, there were about 40.000 Serbs there, and, according to you, before that 140.000 had left Sarajevo. Let me rephrase that. When you arrived in Sarajevo, 40.000 Serbs were there, and 140.000, according to you, had left; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that we estimated, in 1993, that there were up to 40.000 Serbs in the -- the part of Sarajevo controlled by the Bosnian government, but I can't remember the exact statistics now on those who had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated that Karadzic had never expressed or directly denied the people's right to stay in their territories, which means that I never expressly denied the rights of people to stay in any shape or form; is that what you also stated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In our discussion on Monday, I referred to a discussion you had had with one of my superiors about ethnic cleansing in 1993, and you had said at that time that the international community had to carry some of the responsibility for that because they had not agreed to any of the mechanisms for, for example, peaceful exchange of properties and populations of people who wished to leave. And I had said that it was a heavy implication that those who did not leave, who would remain as minorities, say Bosniaks within Serb territory, would be in a -- you know, under pressure or in a difficult position. And you had -- you said on Monday -- you asked, you know, whether they would want to stay in a hostile environment, and then Mr. Sladojevic and I had a little exchange about why that environment might be seen. So I -- I was aware that the forcible removal of populations -- of non-Serb populations from Serb-held territory was an ongoing activity during my period and was widespread as to be, clearly, centrally directed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will challenge that with pleasure during your stay here, or maybe with somebody else. However, what I just quoted is what you stated on 18 September 2003 in the Milosevic case on page 26997, lines from 10 through 14. You said: "I never expressly denied the right of the people to stay." But it seems to me that we agreed on Monday that what I had requested from the international community applied to the individual right of the Serbs to leave an area, and when they did that, not to leave empty-handed, but rather to either be able to exchange property or do something to that effect. You know that our government put a ban on the sale of property, but the international community was in a position to help. Do you agree that the Serbs and Karadzic advocated the individual rights to move -- for the people to move out and exchange properties; they did not advocate a mass relocation of people? You agreed with that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly saw a lot of mass relocation of people. I can't remember whether it was on Monday. But as I moved around the country, whether in the Drina Valley or in the Prijedor area, you would come across large areas where there would be blown-up mosques and blown-up houses. And then I think I said to you on Monday, right, that you would sometimes find hundreds and hundreds of houses blown up, burnt-out, or destroyed, and then one house would not be destroyed in the middle, would have a little garden or something, and then they would have written on it in big paint "Srpska Kuca," meaning this is a Serbian house, indicating that huge numbers of the non-Serb population had been violently expelled. So whatever the stated intention was, what I witnessed was a force -- the results of a forced exodus. And sometimes I would meet these people, themselves, as they -- those who were being expelled would arrive at the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you now is something that you stated about my position. I'm also you again. What was my position? Was my position the way described in the Milosevic case or was my position different? Was my position to advocate the rights of individuals, or, rather, individual right of the people to cross over to a different territory, but with some property to their name, not de-robed of everything they had ever had?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only see the results of the policy, and the results of the policy was the huge-scale violent expulsion of non-Serb populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1993, you saw the consequences of something that had happened in 1999; right? Did you also see the remains of a church that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you saw [as interpreted] any destroyed churches in Trnovo or elsewhere? You said that you saw mosques that had been destroyed. I'm asking you about churches.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I saw destroyed churches during my time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, both Catholic churches and Orthodox Christian churches. I think there was also one at Trnovo. I remember another, I think, near Gorazde, as you came in. Certainly, yeah. And then in Central Bosnia and also near Mostar. Certainly the destruction of Christian places of worship, I was able to witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we agree that what you saw in Prijedor and elsewhere, that that happened a year and a half before you came or, rather, that you only saw the consequences of something that had happened a year and a half before you came; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor, yes, that happened before I was -- I was there. Later, I saw much more recent evidences of forced evictions by the different communities in different parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you will remember you stated that when you had arrived, there were villages around Bijeljina, Muslim villages, which lived happily, and on Monday I asked you to try and remember whether, before your arrival, you learned of a single Serb village in the Muslim or Croatian territory which had persisted and where people continued living unharmed, happily, without any conditions.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to be pedantic, but I don't think I used the word "happily" about them. And, in fact, I think that one of the reasons that we were aware of the Bosniak villages around Bijeljina is because they had expressed their concern about it. And I think I added that while I was not aware of villages, name by name, in territory controlled by the Bosniaks or Croats, that there were tens and tens of thousands of Serbs and Croats and others living in Sarajevo and Tuzla, particularly in these bigger areas. But it's true, when you asked me if I could name a Serb village in Bosnian-government-held territory that had not been ethnically cleansed or which continued to live happily during that period, I could not name one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I said "lived calmly and peacefully," so that may be due to "happily." We don't know what happiness is, so I'm sure I didn't say "happily." Do you agree that the Serbs and Croats who resided in Sarajevo were not there of their own ilk, as we have just established; they were ethnic hostages, as it were? Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that a large number of them wanted to leave, but I think that a large number of Bosniak and other civilians also wanted to leave. My observation did not lead me to the conclusion that they were being held hostage, as you put it, simply because of their nationality. There may have been some cases of that, now that I think about it, but it was not the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we should agree that their ethnic rights may not have been jeopardised, but their civic and human rights were certainly threatened; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that on Mount Romanija -- or let me first ask you, do you know where Mount Romanija is between Pale, Sokolac, and Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were several Muslim villages there which had surrendered their weapons at the very beginning of the war and remained living there without any problems until the very end of the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that was not my experience. My experience, as I drove around Eastern Bosnia, was of the total destruction of villages which had previously been predominantly inhabited by Bosniaks. I remember, when I first drove from Sarajevo to Gorazde, I passed through Rogatica, and you would pass through villages that -- and towns that were completely devastated and bombed, and you would see the minarets of the mosques lying on the ground. So I -- if there were surviving Bosniak villages in that area of Eastern Bosnia which were not destroyed and not living in very difficult circumstances, I admit that I was not aware of them and I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, there were a few villages; Buratisa [phoen], Toravici [phoen], et cetera. We will have a look at that here. But I agree that we were not very good on propaganda. However, did you see Serb villages in the Drina Valley that had been burned?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around Srebrenica, outside of Srebrenica, I -- I had occasion once to visit a tiny community called Kravica. I'm not sure. I think it was predominantly Serb before the war. Is that correct? And in that community, that place, there was evidence of violence against the village and the community, which presumably happened by Bosnian government forces. But I generally can't name the villages one by one, these tiny little communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that General Morillon attended mass burials of Serbs when you got there and later on as well? Also, do you know that before you came, 1.500 Serb civilians were killed around Srebrenica, between Srebrenica and Zvornik, and by the end of the war it was 3.500 Serbs that had been killed? General Morillon honoured us by his presence at these mass burials where these mass graves were. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that in the period prior to my arrival, there had been substantial operations from Bosnian government forces and that civilians -- Serb civilians had been killed. I'm not sure whether the international community was able to independently confirm some of them. I think in the case of this little community, Kravica, there had been some independent international confirmation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Kravica was attacked on Christmas Day, Orthodox Christmas Day, and that Serbs were invariably attacked during Orthodox Christian holidays, whereas during Muslim holidays I publicly issued orders stating that Serbs should not attack? Do you know about that? First of all, was Kravica attacked on Christmas Day out of the blue, without any necessity whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just before I arrived, but that was the report that I received from my colleagues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you about the silo and other prisons where Serbs were held. In one case in 2009, you said that although most of the prisoners in the silo were not killed, they were used to clear minefields, to dig trenches at Treskavica, and so on. Was that your position; was that what you knew?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the grain silos at Tarcin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Tarcin. In relation to the villages we mentioned previously, what I wanted to point out was that the villages that had surrendered their weapons near Sokolac, Rogatica, and Pale, they had not been touched, and we can show that to you on Monday, if you wish. However, I would like to know whether UNPROFOR or NATO ever issued any threats or carried them out because of these crimes committed against Serb villages and Serb civilians, to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I think there was at least one attempt by General Rose to invoke the threat of possible air-strikes against the Bosnian government side, but I think he might be coming at a point, and he can describe that. I now actually admit that I'd forgotten the details. But in general, the threats made by UNPROFOR to use NATO air attacks were overwhelmingly directed at the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you a few questions about cease-fire violations and violations of the demilitarised zone. Do you remember that you stated that there is information showing that during three months in 1993, the Muslim forces violated the cease-fire 196 times?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact numbers, but there were a lot of violations of the cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have the figures from your statements and from your testimony. On the 2nd of February, 1994, up until the 27th of April, 1994, you said that Muslim forces violated the cease-fire 318 times. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it might be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you stated that Karadzic, and now I'm going to speak in English: [In English] "Karadzic issued an order on July the 2nd that Akashi and the UN were to be informed on a daily basis about all Muslim violations of the cease-fire." [Interpretation] That's what you stated in 2003 at the trial of President Milosevic on page 28678. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that these numerous violations were not followed by threats against the Muslim side by UNPROFOR, let alone NATO? Do you agree that they were absolutely spared of that kind of pressure?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR's threats were principally directed at the Bosnian Serbs, though I must say General Rose had a very frank and direct relation with the Bosnian government authorities, too, particularly Dr. Ganic, but it never or very rarely -- very rarely reached the level of direct threats of military strikes which we did use against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put a question to you now. Do you think that that was a legal means for attaining a legal objective, I mean, the fact that we Serbs were under sanctions, the Republic of Serbia, and we, the Serbs, in general, and later on Serbia imposed sanctions on us, and ultimately there were air-strikes? Do you think that that was a legal means? Was it alright to keep us in that situation, under such pressure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Harland has already said on, I think, more than one occasion that he's not a lawyer. And it would be unfair and improper, in my submission, to ask him to make legal conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not as a lawyer, if he can answer the question, based on what he observed at the time, he can answer the question. Otherwise, he may not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that we were acting in accordance with our legal mandate from the United Nations Security Council, particularly, I think, in accordance with Resolution 836 of the Council, when we threatened the use of force, and when we prepared for the use of force, and when, ultimately, in the summer of 1995, we used force on a massive scale, both from the air and from our artillery. I do believe it was consistent with our mandate from the Security Council, which was the basic legal context for our operations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Security Council gave explicit authority to UNPROFOR to call NATO in for close air support when the UNPROFOR forces are under threat? As for the strategic bombing of the Serbs and in order to change the picture on the ground, the Security Council never actually gave explicit permission for that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Security Council is my boss, so I have to be a little bit careful. But I would say that clarity is not the greatest of the Security Council's virtues. But in Resolution 836, in operative paragraphs 5, 9, and 10, there are references to the use of all necessary means to deter attacks by the Bosnian Serb party against six designated safe areas. And we sought not to have to use force on an extreme scale. But in the end we came to the conclusion that the killing and the suffering of the war could not be ended unless we used our mandate to its maximum extent, and, therefore, UNPROFOR quietly prepared the ground in 1995, without telling anybody, for very wide-scale use of air and artillery attacks. But I believe that those air and artillery attacks, which were successful in their objectives, were consistent with Resolution 836, even though it involved hitting targets such as the bridges over the River Drina and communication facilities that were not immediately in the tactical area surrounding the six designated safe areas referred to. But I say this with great hesitation in a room full of lawyers, but we can, presumably, look at that resolution and other resolutions at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will discuss that and reach some agreement. Do you remember that General Mladic said to General Wahlgren and others that whenever his soldiers opened fire at the UN, that they can respond freely, and strongly at that, and that our acceptance of close air support was unopposed, we did not grumble about that? However, I am a bit confused that UNPROFOR was preparing strategic bombing in order to change the situation on the ground and with a view to reaching a political solution. We knew that, but we did not know on which basis that was being done. Can you help us on that? On which basis did UNPROFOR prepare that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR came to the conclusion in the summer of 1995 that it could not discharge its mandate to protect the civilian populations of these six designated areas without using its mandate to use all necessary means to maximum effect. It was, therefore, decided that preparations would be made for air and artillery attacks far beyond just close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I think that we saw yesterday that that had been done with a view to bringing the war to an end, and that Markale -- isn't that right? You do agree, don't you, that the plan for strategic -- of strategic bombing was made with a view to having the war brought to an end?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly our view by that point that we could not discharge our mandate unless we directly helped to end the war. So, yes, UNPROFOR decided that it had to use the "all necessary means" described in Resolution 836 and elsewhere to protect the civilian populations through the extreme means of ending the war, including by force. But our understanding was that was, in some ways, the intention of Resolution 836, so yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, hearing the interpretation and looking at the transcript, I note that "Markale" is somewhat hanging in the question. Did you ask any question regarding Markale?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to go back to that, because Mr. Harland said yesterday that that operation had been prepared for weeks in advance, with an intention that they probably considered to be noble, to end the war, and that Markale was used as a pretext, and it was as if it had fallen from heaven in order to have a pretext for the strategic bombing at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly. The position of UNPROFOR was that we needed to be in a position to apply force, directly and on a large scale, in order to insist on the compliance with our mandate to protect civilians. If anything happened that would indicate that the Serb side was not respecting our absolute insistence that the civilian population be protected, that instead of simply having a threat, we would implement -- we would initiate those attacks from the air and from the artillery. And what I indicated yesterday was that the Markale massacre had not been foreseen by anybody, but was certainly such an attack as would trigger not just a threat, but the actual implementation of widespread attacks against the Serb forces by the UNPROFOR artillery, the Rapid Reaction Force, and by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to that, with your permission. Now let us see what your position was. I think I can actually quote this; namely, that the Bosnians just wanted breaks, as far as cease-fires were concerned. However, if there weren't any positive negotiations, they would go on fighting. And then I quote: [In English] "The Serbs said that either there is a war -- no agreement or that there is no war, a complete cessation of hostilities." [Interpretation] You correctly interpreted my position there; namely, that Muslims use cease-fires for consolidation and that, on the other hand, we get weaker day after day and that we want either war or peace, not to allow them cease-fires that would make them stronger and stronger, better armed, et cetera. [In English] Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, this is page 96, line 9, yesterday's transcript. You say: [In English] "This takes a minute or two, if that's okay. There, General Smith had a plan to end the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or at least a series of initiatives that would contribute to the end of the war. And central to those initiatives was the need to direct NATO air-strikes against the Bosnian Serbs on a massive scale." [Interpretation] So it is quite clear that without Markale and without an awareness of some intentions of ours to take anything, a plan was being drawn up: [In English] "Now nobody could predict when these Markale atrocities happened, that this would be the incident that would trigger these air-strikes." [Interpretation] Now I would be interested in the following,

utterances.speaker: MR. HARLAND
utterances.text: Did the Security Council ever pass a decision for the UN forces to change the balance of power in the field, that is to say, to weaken one side, in order to have a solution finally found? I understand that have you to talk about your bosses, but it's not the same persons. The persons who were there then haven't been there for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could no longer implement our mandate to protect the civilian populations without having the most -- without making maximum use of the mandate we had received from the Security Council. If we had gone to the Security Council, in advance of the operation we launched on the night of the 29th and 30th of August, and had explicitly asked for their legal imprimatur in advance, I don't know. Perhaps you are correct. The mandate was relatively obscure, and -- but it gave very broad goals and very broad authorities, and in the end, we felt we could only reach those broad goals by the extensive use of those authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harland, don't you think that less force could have been used, and less resources, had you made it possible for the protected areas to be demilitarised? We see that we do agree that we were being killed from Srebrenica and Zepa every day. Wouldn't it have been easier to pass and carry out that kind of resolution, demilitarisation of the protected areas, or safe havens? That was explicitly ordered by the Security Council, instead of bombing the Serb side. Why were these safe havens not demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the first question, I would say that UNPROFOR was extremely patient. In fact, after Markale 1, which is one year and a half before we finally launched these major operations, there had been a very active consideration of using air power on a large scale then, but we were always attempting to discharge our mandate, to deliver humanitarian aid, and to help the sides reach a cease-fire, in the hope that they could reach a negotiated settlement without having to use force. And I think, frankly, if the massacre at Srebrenica had not happened, it is unlikely that UNPROFOR would have taken the final decisive steps to prepare the large military operations that came in August and September and ended the -- helped to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I take you back to the issue of protected areas. What I'm putting to you, sir, is this: Those protected areas did not protect the civilians, but, rather, the Muslim fighters who, as the Secretary-General of the United Nations had established, opened fire on Serbs and then returned to the protection of the United Nations, why they were not demilitarised in keeping with the resolution of the Security Council which ordered for these protected areas to be fully demilitarised? Why was that not implemented?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have these resolutions in front of me, but if I remember correctly, the resolutions, I think probably 824, but maybe 819 or 836, calls for the withdrawal of all forces except Bosnian government forces. I don't have the text and I don't recall the exact words, but my memory is that the mandate -- the obligation placed on UNPROFOR to try to deter Serb attacks by all means necessary was not predicated on the Bosnian government's previous demilitarisation of the areas. We certainly supported the demilitarisation of the areas, and we pursued negotiations in that direction, but I have a feeling that the language of the resolution does refer to the withdrawal of your forces, but does not refer to the withdrawal or removal of the Bosnian government forces. But I could be wrong. Those resolutions I haven't looked at for a long, long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] You are excused, because you said that you are not military expert.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, can the Court please produce 1D953.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While this is being done, let me remind you that safe havens or safe zones, according to the International Rules of War, have to be agreed between the parties. They have to be delineated or delimitated, which means that borders have to be agreed, and they have to be demilitarised inside so as to make sure that no threat comes from the inside of them on the surroundings, and vice versa. As one of the conditions is met and the is another not, you will agree with me that the military and the civilians who suffered daily killings and attacks from that safe zone cannot be satisfied? This is a document entitled "An agreement on the demilitarised zones of Srebrenica and Zepa," and this was signed by General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993, in the presence of General Philippe Morillon. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your first question is -- is, No. I mean, you and I are two of the only people in this room who are not lawyers. But my understanding is that what you are referring to, which is the safety zones described in the protocol -- is it the 1947 Protocols Additional to the Geneva Conventions, the 1st Protocol with respect to international armed conflicts, but I think the same provision appears in the protocol on non-international conflict, describe safety zones which can be agreed between the parties, and it describes demilitarisation, and it describes markings with red crosses, and so on. Whereas what was created by the Security Council, at least in English, has a completely different name. They're called safe areas, and there is no reference that is saying that these are the same as those safety zones referred to which -- in the Geneva Conventions, which I think are envisaged as very tiny things, basically for the protection of hospitals and similar; that what was being described by the Security Council was a completely different concept from which the Security Council demanded that the Serbs withdraw their forces, but did not demand that the Bosniaks demilitarise or withdraw their forces. Now, I don't claim that this was a very intellectually coherent mandate. It was full of problems. The agreement which you have pointed to is not, in our view, determinative on the Security Council. There was a negotiation going on between General Wahlgren -- General Mladic, Gvero, and General Halilovic were there, and General Wahlgren. But I think our view was that whether -- it was obviously good if that agreement would be implemented, though most agreements in Bosnia and Herzegovina were wildly violated by all sides. And, in any case, our view was that the Security Council resolution calling for the Serbs to withdraw would have legal effect on us and oblige us to continue, irrespective of that agreement. But now we are wading into a legal swamp and are likely to get caught by our peers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the first page and the preamble, which mentions all those things that I am talking about. And then I would like to go to page 3. In this document, will you see that we're both right. However, the order is in my favour. Article 11, please. Page 3, Article 11. When the Serbs withdrew weapons, let me read in English: [In English] "When both sides in the presence of UNPROFOR agree that the operation has been completed, all heavy weapons and units that constitute a menace to the demilitarised zone which will have been established in Zepa and Srebrenica will be withdrawn. Heavy weapons and tanks will be concentrated in limited areas that will be monitored by UNPROFOR and, in principle, out of range of the demilitarised zone. Infantry will be withdrawn to a range from which their weapons cannot constitute a menace to the security of the demilitarised zone, in principle, one and a half kilometres." [Interpretation] Up to Article 11, there are explanations of the conditions for the withdrawal of the Serb troops. Complete demilitarisation. Nobody but the police. Very small numbers of them could wear a uniform. And then the Serb forces were supposed to withdraw at a distance of one and a half kilometres and put heavy weapons out of range. And the Serbs even did that. However, they suffered daily losses, on average a soldier a day, and some civilians. And the Trial Chamber will have an opportunity to see the atrocities that we suffered from the demilitarised zones. Tell us, please, why did not UNPROFOR demilitarise those zones? The first ten articles and the conditions set out therein had to be met in order for Article 11, and the conditions therein could be met; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The agreement -- nobody wanted the agreement honoured more than us. But that agreement is an agreement between -- if I remember correctly, between General Mladic and General Halilovic, in our presence. It is one of hundreds of agreements made between the Bosnian -- or at least dozens of agreements between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serbs, which were subject to absolutely continuous violations on all sides. Our view was whether or not they made or honoured an agreement between themselves, we had a mandate flowing from the Security Council. To be absolutely frank, we were not happy with the mandate from the Security Council. The mandate from the Security Council asked us to deter attacks by your forces. We said, If you want us to do that, we would need 36.000 troops. We officially said that. The Secretary-General said that to the Security Council, and the Security Council did not provide the troops. So we had only a tiny amount of people, so obviously we pursued everything we could within our means to make this -- to fulfill our mandate by encouraging these sorts of agreement. But, frankly, we were not very surprised when all sides were in massive violation of them. And in the end, the mandate from the Security Council to deter attacks still continued, even though we had not the troops that were needed given to us by the countries which gave us that mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree with me that you should have thwarted attacks against the Serb civilians from the protected areas under your protection? Under whose protection were we? How was it possible to prevent the attacks on us? Could you have used NATO? Could you have threatened us with NATO, as did you when you decided to bomb the Serbs? How come you did not have the power to put Muslims before -- an alternative. Either you're going to stop attacking the Serb villages, or, alternatively, we're going to stop protecting your protected zone.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mandate from the Security Council, like it or not, was to designate six Bosnian government, Bosniak-majority areas as safe areas that would be safe from attack by your forces. The Security Council had come to that decision for its own reason; presumably, because they felt that your forces were overwhelmingly militarily dominant and were conducting a campaign against those six areas and others that required some sort of international action. So the Security Council mandate did not ask of UNPROFOR the sort of equivalence that you are referring to. And when General Rose considered seriously the use of air attacks against the Bosnian government when it had considered -- had committed certain violations, I think he found that it was not politically possible to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we agree that you didn't have the mandate to bomb the Serbs within the range of strategic bombing; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now -- can this agreement between Mladic and Halilovic, in the presence of Morillon, be admitted? Can we please look at page 4 to display the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question, can we agree that you didn't have the mandate to bomb the Serbs within the range of strategic bombing, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer to that question is, No. On the contrary, our understanding of the mandate is that we did, if necessary, have the mandate to use all necessary means to bring about the intended goals of the mandate, and in the end we reached the conclusion we could only do that by bringing the war to an end by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that there is a decision of the Security Council that peacekeeping forces should become peace-imposing forces? Is there a document to such an effect?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- first of all, I have already said that the mandate of UNPROFOR is relatively obscure. In my view, it was an expression of the lowest common denominator of international will to address the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Specifically to answer your question, UNPROFOR was never really a peacekeeping force because there was no peace to keep. There was a war, a raging war, with up to -- over 300.000 combatants, and we were a small force of less than 10 per cent of that, dropped into the middle of it, and there was no peace to keep. And there was a mandate later in the war. There was a mandate under Resolution 836 to use all necessary means. The problem was that we didn't have the necessary means. And if General Smith had not worked very carefully to create the conditions to deal with these problems we discussed yesterday, the Mogadishu problem and the hostage problem, he would never have been able to reach the successful conclusion that was reached. And even so, it happened far too late.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could page 4 please be displayed, the signature page, and can this document please be admitted. And now can the Court please produce 1D978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we see General Morillon, General Mladic, and General Halilovic's signatures? Do you agree that this page is part of the same document? Right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the agreement please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there will be an objection to this. It will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next document, 978?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next one is 978, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just the first paragraph, on the 27th of June, 1995, and this document was produced by the Muslim Army, by the 2nd Corps. The BiH Army, the commander of the 2nd Corps, "Strictly confidential," and so on and so forth. And this was sent to -- and here's what it says: "On the 26th of June, 1995," which was some 10 days before the operation in Srebrenica, "in the morning hours of 26 June 1995, our forces attacked from the Srebrenica sector and set fire to the village of Visnjica. According to as yet unconfirmed intelligence, the Chetniks," which means Serbs, "suffered casualties among the civilian population." Which ethnic community and which army would have tolerated any such thing, despite any resolutions of the United Nations? Do you agree with me that we were fully in our right not to tolerate that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly agree with you that this appears to be a violation of the agreement you referred to, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D136.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 1D980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While this is being done, do you agree with me that there is a complete agreement about the fact that the original Serb plan was not to take over Srebrenica, but to separate the enclaves and to reducing them to the previously-agreed borders, as per this agreement? Your own sources say that. They say that there was no plan to take over, that it was a sudden development, because Srebrenica was no longer defended after they had withdrawn from Srebrenica. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say that the intention of the Serb forces was not simply to return the safe areas to the size they had been at the moment of their creation by the Security Council. On the contrary, General Mladic even agreed -- even told General Smith that the hope, or the expectation, or the plan of the Serbs was to reduce them to very tiny areas. I forget what, one and a half kilometres or three kilometres across, or something much smaller than at the moment of demarcation. As to whether or not the Serb intention had actually been to -- at the outset of the operation against Srebrenica, had been to take it completely and to massacre its population, or whether that decision was taken opportunistically at a late stage, I'm not sure that I am in a position to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go on talking about that. But the fact is that your information, the information in the possession of the United Nations, was to reduce the areas to an area less than agreed. The Serbs claim that it was within the agreed area, and they left the areas to torch Serbian villages. Their goal was to link up all the Serbian territories and tie up the Serb forces around Sarajevo, where the summer offensive was underway in 1995. I'm sure that you observed -- you were an eye-witness to all that offensive. Do you agree with all of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with it all, except for the comment that the Serbs claimed that it was -- that they only intended to reduce the safe areas to the agreed area. I think the Serbs explicitly told General Smith that they intended to reduce them much further than that. In my written testimony, there is a reference to an order. I think it's signed by yourself, a certain Directive 7, which also directly states that the goal is to make life unlivable in the -- in at least the three eastern enclaves. I don't have the document in front of me, but I recall having been -- having looked at it during the process of research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave it for the subject of next week?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harland can be excused. I hope you have a good, refreshing weekend.
